title: Meteorites You Can Hold
subtitle: Older than Earth
yt_title: You Can Hold Something Older Than Earth 🪨 | Ep. 109 #shorts
description:
Episode 109 of a daily journey through the universe. 🪨
We hold a meteorite: the difference between a meteor and a meteorite, tons of space dust falling on Earth every day, the 60-ton Hoba iron, meteorites from Mars and the Moon, and grains of stardust older than the Sun.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 110: Next stop, Tunguska. The day a forest was flattened by the sky.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

Images: NASA (public domain)
Narration: AI voice

#space #meteorite #astronomy #shorts #science #nasa

segments.text: Episode one hundred and nine. Next stop... meteorites you can hold.
A space rock flying through space is a meteoroid. When it burns in our sky, it's a meteor. If it lands, it's a meteorite.
segments.headline: Meteor or meteorite?

segments.text: Every day, Earth collects tons of space dust and rock. Most of it is tiny grains, falling unnoticed.
Some meteorites are mostly iron and nickel, the cores of broken asteroids.
segments.headline: Pieces of asteroid cores

segments.text: The biggest one ever found is Hoba, in Namibia. About sixty tons of iron. It never even left a crater.
We've even found meteorites from Mars and the Moon, blasted off by impacts and landed on Earth.
segments.headline: From Mars and the Moon

segments.text: Some stony meteorites are about four and a half billion years old. Older than any rock on Earth.
Inside some, scientists found tiny grains of stardust that are even older than our Sun.
segments.headline: Older than the Sun

segments.text: Want to touch one? Many science museums let you. You'd be touching the birth of the solar system.
segments.headline: Touch one yourself

segments.text: Tomorrow, we go back to nineteen oh eight. A blast in Siberia knocked down eighty million trees. Follow, so you don't miss episode one hundred and ten.
